growth_story.headline: Greece's euro-era boom ended in a deep debt crisis; growth returned from 2016, but income per person is still below its 2007 peak.
growth_story.arc: From 1990 to 1997 income per person grew 0.7 percent a year, and the sources say little about this era. Growth sped up to 3.8 percent a year in 1998–2007, as euro entry and cheap foreign credit fed spending, much of it by the government, the IMF says. When the global financial crisis threatened that financing, Greece lost market access in 2010, and income per person fell 3.5 percent a year in 2008–2015, with the worst year, 2011, at -9.7 percent. Growth came back at 2.1 percent a year in 2016–2025, despite a fall of 9.0 percent in the 2020 pandemic year; for the years since 2021 the IMF credits investment backed by EU recovery funds and foreign investment, a rebound in tourism and reforms. Even so, income per person in 2025 was 8.6 percent below its 2007 peak, about where it first was in 2004.

threads.title: Euro entry and a borrowed boom
threads.text: After Greece joined the euro, it could borrow abroad cheaply, and government spending and household credit grew fast. Prices rose faster than in the rest of the euro area, and the economy lost competitiveness.

threads.text: The global crisis of 2008 threatened the foreign financing behind the boom, and in 2010 Greece lost access to markets. The recession that followed was deep, with very high unemployment, and investment fell from 25.5 percent of GDP in 2007 to 11.0 percent in 2019.

threads.text: Since 2021, the IMF says, investment backed by the EU's Next Generation EU recovery funds and foreign investment, a rebound in tourism and reforms have driven growth. Investment rose from 11.0 percent of GDP in 2019 to 16.9 percent in 2025, but the IMF still calls it low.

threads.title: A shrinking working-age population
threads.text: The number of people of working age has been falling and is projected to keep falling. The IMF links this, along with low labour force participation and slow productivity growth, to slower growth ahead.

growth_story.tension: The IMF describes a strong recovery since 2021. The data agree on the rebound, but much of it is a bounce back from the 2020 fall: income per person in 2025 was still 8.6 percent below its 2007 peak, and over 2006–2025 it grew only 0.1 percent a year. The sources also describe credit picking up again, while bank credit to the private sector kept falling as a share of GDP through 2024.
